title: Fast zkSNARK proofs for large language model inference
excerpt: Anthropic’s FlashProve generates zkSNARK proofs at 110 tokens per second with 19 MB proof size for a 400B-parameter model.
body:
FlashProve puts provable inference within reach of today’s biggest language models  

When a user asks an AI assistant for advice, the response arrives without any way to confirm which model actually produced it. A routing service could swap in a cheaper model, or an attacker could tamper with the token stream and still deliver plausible text. The problem is not just academic: independent evaluators need to certify that a benchmark runs on the advertised model, and enterprises that pay per-token want assurance that they are not being short-changed.  

Cryptographic proofs of inference answer that need. By committing to a specific model and then generating a proof that each output came from the committed model, a provider can let anyone verify the provenance of a response.

The Anthropic team’s recent post, *Progress on provable inference for large language models* ([source](https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference)), describes a system called FlashProve that makes this approach practical for a 400-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model. The post will walk through the performance numbers, the formal security guarantees expressed in Lean, and three concrete ways the proofs could be used in production.

## Near-real-time proof generation on a 400 B model  

FlashProve targets the Llama 4 Maverick mixture-of-experts model, which contains 400 billion parameters. The authors quantized the weights to 4 bits and performed integer arithmetic during the prefill stage. Under those conditions a single NVIDIA H100 GPU produces zkSNARK proofs at roughly 110 tokens per second. A request that generates 1,024 tokens yields a proof of about 19 MB.  

The proof-generation cost is 70, 95 × the GPU time required to run the model itself with vLLM, a common open-source inference library. Prior open-source provable-inference systems were orders of magnitude slower and could not keep up with real-time inference at any comparable scale. FlashProve achieves its speed by applying state-of-the-art cryptographic tools in novel ways and by aligning the proof pipeline tightly with the model’s execution graph.  

## Formal, auditable security claims in Lean  

Speed alone does not guarantee trust. FlashProve therefore publishes top-level security statements in Lean, a formal verification language. The Lean theorems prove that the zkSNARK hides the model’s weights while still allowing a verifier to check that a given output matches the committed model. Hiding the model’s architecture is not a goal of the system, and the source explicitly notes that the proofs do not conceal architecture.  

By releasing both the Lean source files and an interactive visualizer, the authors let external auditors trace each step of the argument. This transparency addresses a common criticism of cryptographic systems: opaque optimizations that are hard to evaluate in large pipelines. The combination of a fast C++ verifier and a provably correct verifier implemented in Lean gives operators a choice between raw speed and formal assurance.  

## Real-world scenarios that benefit from provable inference  

Provable inference is not a theoretical curiosity; it fits several practical needs. FlashProve’s proof size (≈19 MB) and verification speed make these scenarios feasible:  

1. Benchmark integrity, Independent evaluators can attach a proof to every response during a model-evaluation campaign. The proof guarantees that the tokens came from the exact version advertised, preventing “model swapping” that could skew results.  

2. Third-party routing assurance, Clients that route requests through a cloud provider or API gateway can demand a proof alongside each response. If the proof fails, the client knows the tokens were not generated by the paid-for model, protecting against cost-saving substitutions.  

3. Tamper-evident deployments, In security-sensitive environments, an attacker who intercepts and modifies the token stream cannot produce a valid zkSNARK without access to the committed model’s weights. The verifier will reject the tampered output, alerting the system to a breach.  

These use cases rely on the fact that verification is orders of magnitude cheaper than proof generation. The C++ verifier can check a 19 MB proof in a fraction of a second on modest hardware, making it suitable for on-device or edge deployments.  

## Open-source release and future work  

All FlashProve artifacts are released under the Apache 2.0 license: the prover, two verifiers (fast C++ and Lean-based), the Lean proofs, and a protocol specification document. The authors describe the post as “intermediate progress” rather than a finished research agenda, inviting the community to build on the work.  

The source notes that the system does not aim to hide the model’s architecture, and it does not address the confidentiality of training data. Future research could explore extensions that protect both weights and architecture, or that integrate differential-privacy guarantees for the data that generated the model.  

## The takeaway  

FlashProve shows that zkSNARK-based provable inference can run at near-real-time speeds on a 400 billion-parameter language model while providing formally verified security guarantees in Lean. For anyone who needs cryptographic proof that a specific LLM generated a response, whether for compliance, benchmarking, or anti-tampering, FlashProve offers a practical, auditable foundation that can be integrated into existing AI pipelines.
